title: Nkatenkwan from Asamankese
author: Juliet Asamoah
desc: Learnt from a cook in Asamankese — palm oil with the groundnut paste until the oils start to separate, about ten okro, and a litre of hot water.
longDesc: This version was learnt in Asamankese in the Eastern Region and it is the only documented groundnut soup that fries the paste in palm oil before anything else goes in: heat the palm oil, add the groundnut paste and work it until the oils start to separate, then the tomatoes, then thirty minutes of simmering. The cooked vegetables are ground and returned, and it continues until the chicken is tender and the oils collect on the surface. A litre of hot water is added. Roughly three hundred grams of groundnuts and about ten okro — most of the rest is unquantified, honestly so.
ingredients: About 300 g groundnuts, or peanut butter
steps: Steam the chicken with the aromatics.
Make the groundnut paste, if starting from whole groundnuts.
Heat the palm oil and add the paste, working it until the oils start to separate.
Add the tomatoes and simmer 30 minutes.
Grind the cooked vegetables and return them to the pot.
Continue until the chicken is tender and the oils collect on the surface.
chefTips: Frying the groundnut paste in palm oil first is unique to this version, and it is the step that gives the deepest flavour of any documented groundnut soup. The oils separating at this early stage is the cue.
Note that the oils separate twice in this recipe — once when you fry the paste, and again at the end when they collect on the surface. Both are cues and both matter.
Steam the chicken rather than boiling it. Less water in at the start means a more concentrated soup.
About ten okro is the printed amount. It is the only documented groundnut soup besides GHA015 to include okra.
Three hundred grams of groundnuts for a whole chicken sits in the middle of the documented range, and if you grind them yourself you get a far better soup than peanut butter gives.
Grind the cooked vegetables and return them — the same remove-blend-return technique the light soups use.
Most of this recipe is unquantified and that is recorded rather than filled in. Palm oil, ginger, scotch bonnet and the stock cube carry no amounts in the source.
commonMistakes: Skipping the palm oil fry and adding the paste to liquid.
Boiling the chicken rather than steaming it.
Adding the litre of hot water before the vegetables are returned.
Serving before the oils collect on the surface.
Assuming the unquantified items are negligible — the palm oil in particular is substantial.
sources: Adapted from 'Ghanaian Nkatenkwan', talkingoffood.com, in the series 'A Year in Chicken Soup'. No date is shown.

BYLINE UNRESOLVED, and stated as such. One fetch returned the byline 'Hattie Garlick'. A second returned the recipe credit: 'learnt from Mama Juliet', described as 'a large, indomitable woman from Asamankese, a small town in the eastern region of Ghana', where 'contributor Connie Smith spent three months'. So there are potentially three people involved — a site author, a contributor, and the cook the recipe came from — and the ownership of talkingoffood.com could not be established. All three names are recorded; none is asserted as the author. The cook, Mama Juliet of Asamankese, is credited in the display author field as the source of the method.

Ingredients exactly as printed, and NOTE that only two carry quantities: A whole chicken; About 300g of groundnuts (or peanut butter); Okro about 10; Scotch bonnets, palm oil, stock cube; Can of tomatoes; 3 onions; Root ginger, water, rice.

Method as printed: steam the chicken with aromatics; make the groundnut paste; heat palm oil, add the paste until 'oils start to separate', add the tomatoes, and simmer 30 minutes; grind the cooked vegetables and return them; continue until the chicken is tender and oils collect on the surface. One litre of hot water is added.

THE FULL ORIGINAL WORDING WAS NOT OBTAINED, and the quantities above are what survived two fetches. Treat the unquantified items as genuinely unquantified in the source rather than lost in transcription.

DOUBLE OIL CUE, which is what distinguishes this version: 'oils start to separate' when the paste is fried in palm oil at the start, and 'oils collect on surface' at the end. No other documented groundnut soup frying the paste in palm oil first was found.

ASAMANKESE is in the Eastern Region, which is Akan territory — the basis for the community attribution above. It is also the region where Osseo-Asare records first meeting aprapransa under its Twi name (GHA010).
PEANUT RATIO POSITION: 'about 300g of groundnuts' for a whole chicken. For the full six-source spread see the sources at GHA013.

A NOTE ON WHY THIS IS PUBLISHED DESPITE THE BYLINE PROBLEM: the method is attributed to a named cook in a named town, the palm-oil-first technique is documented nowhere else, and the two oil cues are real observable endpoints. The byline confusion is in the publishing chain rather than in the provenance of the cooking, and it is stated openly above.
reheating: Gentle heat with water to loosen.
healthBenefits: Groundnuts ground fresh retain more vitamin E than commercial peanut butter.
Red palm oil supplies provitamin-A carotenoids.
Okra adds soluble fibre and folate.
High in protein from the whole chicken.
culturalNote: A recipe learnt over three months in one woman's kitchen in Asamankese reads differently from one developed for a magazine — it is mostly technique and cues, with almost no numbers, because that is how it was taught. The palm-oil-first step is the kind of thing that only survives being learnt in person, and it is the single best idea in the documented record for this soup.
